claims.text: Premelting and melting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed by the degree of atomic-scale short-range chemical ordering.
Ni-centered interactions play an especially important role in governing the thermal response.
Increasing temperature gradually disorders the short-range chemical order.
Disordering of short-range order decreases local cohesive energy.
The decrease in local cohesive energy triggers premelting below the bulk melting point.
Short-range-order breakdown dictates nucleation of the liquid phase.
The synthesis and cooling history can produce different initial degrees of short-range order in otherwise chemically homogeneous nanoparticles.
Controlled slow cooling enhances short-range order in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Rapid quenching produces a comparatively randomized elemental distribution with minimal short-range order.
The relevant structural mediator consists of local Ni-centered clusters involving Fe, Cr, Co, and Cu.
Local short-range order raises the energy barrier for atomic rearrangements during heating.
Breakdown of short-range order produces a spatially heterogeneous decrease in cohesive energy.
Sites where short-range order breaks down undergo localized premelting and become precursors to complete melting.
Nanoparticles with greater initial short-range order will have a delayed onset of premelting relative to randomized nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with greater initial short-range order will exhibit more spatially heterogeneous premelting.
Nanoparticles with greater initial short-range order will exhibit a broader melting regime.
Randomized nanoparticles will melt more uniformly and possibly at a lower temperature than short-range-ordered nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to approximately 10–100 nm particles under thermal conditions that permit measurable short-range-order evolution.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to bulk or micrometer-scale samples or when processing erases detectable chemical order.
Failure of verified high-SRO particles to differ significantly in premelting or melting behavior from randomized controls would falsify the governing-SRO hypothesis.
